As summer gives way to fall, many homeowners begin preparing for seasonal changes around the house. From swapping out summer wardrobes to tackling fall home maintenance projects, this time of year is about preparing for what’s ahead. It is also a good time to think about your home’s energy use.


While fall is often one of the mildest seasons of the year, it serves as a transition between summer cooling and winter heating. Understanding how your energy use changes throughout the year can help you prepare for the months ahead and make more informed energy decisions.


**Why Does Energy Use Change Throughout the Year?**


Your home’s energy use isn’t the same every month. Seasonal factors influence how much energy your home consumes and when that energy is used.


Some of the biggest factors include:


- Outdoor temperatures
- Heating and cooling needs
- Changes in daylight hours
- Time spent at home
- Seasonal activities and routines


During the summer, air conditioning often becomes one of the largest contributors to household energy use. In the winter, heating systems typically take center stage. Even homes that use natural gas or another fuel source for heating still rely on electricity to power thermostats, blowers, pumps, and other equipment. Residential energy use varies significantly by season, with demand increasing during both the hottest and coldest times of the year as homeowners work to maintain comfort indoors.


**Fall Is an Important Transition Season**


Fall is sometimes referred to as a “shoulder season” because it falls between the high energy demands of summer and winter. You may find yourself using air conditioning less frequently while beginning to use your heating system for the first time in months. At the same time, shorter days mean lights are turned on earlier, and more time spent indoors can increase the use of electronics, appliances, and hot water.


Because the temperatures are generally milder, fall gives homeowners an opportunity to evaluate changing energy needs before winter arrives. These gradual changes can seem small at first, but together they signal the start of a new energy-use pattern that often continues through the winter months.


**What Drives Higher Energy Use During Colder Months?**


Eventually, as temperatures begin to drop, homes often require more energy to stay comfortable. Several factors can contribute to increased energy use, including:


Heating Your Home: Heating systems generally work harder and run longer as outdoor temperatures decrease.


Shorter Days: With fewer hours of daylight, households often rely more on indoor lighting during the morning and evening.


More Time Indoors: Colder weather naturally brings many activities inside, which can mean more use of televisions, artificial lighting, computers, kitchen appliances, and other electronics.


Seasonal Gatherings and Cooking: Holiday meals, baking, entertaining guests, and additional laundry can all contribute to higher household energy use.


Understanding what drives winter energy use can help explain why household consumption often looks different in January than it did in July.


**How to Prepare for the Change in Seasons**


While fall is a great time to learn about changing energy patterns, it’s also a good opportunity to take steps that can help prepare your home for the seasonal changes.


Conduct a Home Energy Audit


A home energy audit can identify areas where your home may be losing energy. Whether you conduct an audit yourself or hire a professional, an energy assessment can identify opportunities to improve efficiency before winter arrives.


Take Advantage of Mild Temperatures


One of the benefits of fall is the opportunity to enjoy comfortable outdoor temperatures. On mild days, open windows to bring in fresh air instead of relying on your heating or cooling system. Natural ventilation can help keep your home comfortable while reducing HVAC use.


Switch to LED Lighting


As daylight becomes shorter, lighting often plays a larger role in household energy use. If you haven’t already made the switch, LED light bulbs use up to 75% less energy and last 25 times longer than traditional incandescent bulbs.


Seal Windows and Doors


Small air leaks around windows and doors allow warm air to escape once temperatures begin to drop. Sealing gaps and drafts before winter arrives can help improve comfort and reduce the amount of energy needed to heat your home.


**Prepare for the Season Ahead**


By understanding how and why energy consumption changes throughout the year, you can better prepare for the colder season. Paying attention to seasonal patterns can help you understand how your home uses energy all year long.


Whether you’re turning on the heat for the first time, adjusting to shorter days, or simply planning for winter, fall is the perfect time to take a closer look at the role energy plays in keeping your home comfortable.
